details: Cs-134/Cs-137 activity ratio = primary Chernobyl nuclear forensic signature: Cs-134 (t½=2.065yr) is NOT a direct fission product in significant quantities; produced by: Cs-133 (stable fission product) + thermal neutron → Cs-134 + γ; i.e., Cs-134 is an ACTIVATION product of stable Cs-133 that accumulated in fuel during reactor operation; Cs-134 production proportional to: Cs-133 inventory × neutron flux × time; burnup = ~15,000 MWd/tHM for Unit 4 at accident; calculated Cs-134/Cs-137 activity ratio at shutdown = ~0.60; decay-corrected to May 6 1986 (peak deposition day): = 0.57; this ratio is UNIQUE to Chernobyl fuel burnup history; weapons fallout has NO Cs-134 (weapons are single-pulse; no Cs-133 accumulation)
chernobyl_application: Forensic applications of Cs-134/Cs-137 ratio: (1) distinguish Chernobyl contamination from weapons test fallout (ratio=0 for weapons); (2) date the contamination event (ratio decreases with time as Cs-134 decays faster: 0.57×e^(-t×0.336) from 1986); (3) current 2026 ratio: 0.57 × exp(-40 × 0.336) = 0.57 × e^(-13.44) = 0.57 × 1.33×10⁻⁶ ≈ negligible (Cs-134 essentially all decayed by 2026; 19 half-lives); therefore: post-2000 samples with NO Cs-134 but positive Cs-137 = Chernobyl origin confirmed from ratio=0 (old source) vs weapons fallout (same ratio=0 = ambiguous); other Chernobyl fingerprints needed for current samples
source: nuclear_fuel_cycle_burnup_REAL.csv; fission_product_yields_REAL.csv; atmospheric_transport_plume_REAL.csv; IAEA Nuclear Forensics Glossary 2019

details: Chernobyl attribution in 2026 samples: Cs-134 fully decayed (t½=2.065yr; 40yr = 19.4 half-lives; 2.5×10⁻⁶ of initial activity remains = below detection everywhere); therefore current forensic attribution relies on: (1) geographic distribution matching 1986 deposition maps; (2) Cs-137/Sr-90 ratio at deposition locations matches known release fractions; (3) Am-241 presence (growing from Pu-241; no other significant source); (4) Pu-239/240 ratio: Pu-240/Pu-239 activity ratio = 0.30-0.45 for reactor-grade Pu (burnup-dependent) vs ~0.04 for weapons-grade Pu (highly enriched); (5) U-235 depletion pattern (below natural 0.72%); (6) spatial correlation with Chernobyl plume trajectory
chernobyl_application: Pu-240/Pu-239 ratio: reactor Pu = high burnup → high Pu-240; weapons Pu = low burnup (<200 MWd/tHM) → low Pu-240 (<7%); Chernobyl Pu: 15,000 MWd/tHM → Pu-240/(Pu-239+240) ~25-30%; this is definitive against weapons origin; Am-241 in CEZ soils: only source is Pu-241 decay (t½=14.29yr) which is itself from neutron activation chain; Am-241 growing until 2058.7 = unmistakable Chernobyl signature (no weapons test would produce same temporal pattern); CTBTO forensic capability: can distinguish Chernobyl, Fukushima, and weapons test Pu by isotope ratios to within 1 year of irradiation history
source: am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv; nuclear_fuel_cycle_burnup_REAL.csv; ru106_2017_europe_REAL.csv; IAEA Nuclear Forensics Library

details: Ru-106 2017 European event: nuclear forensics case study; 250 TBq Ru-106 detected September-October 2017 across Europe; attribution methodology: (1) isotope: only Ru-106 detected; no co-release of other fission/activation products; suggests reprocessing origin rather than reactor accident (whole-fuel release would include Cs, Sr, I); (2) trajectory: CTBTO FLEXPART backward trajectory from all 30+ detection stations → converging source region = Southern Urals (Mayak PA facility, Chelyabinsk Oblast); (3) timing: first detections September 26-27 → backward transport ~5-7 days → release September 21-22 2017; (4) isotope ratio: Ru-106 only = consistent with Ru-106 target material for Pd-106 production or nuclear fuel reprocessing off-gas; (5) Ru-106/Ru-103 ratio = no Ru-103 detected → rules out recent criticality event (Ru-103 t½=39d would persist)
chernobyl_application: Russia denied for 18 months; IRSN (France) published analysis April 2019 attributing to Mayak; France's ACF (fuel fabrication company at Elektrostal) partially acknowledged; key forensic point: single-isotope Ru-106 release = UNIQUELY consistent with spent fuel reprocessing or Ru-106 target material separation; would not occur in reactor accident (would see Cs-137, I-131 also); forensic methodology: CTBTO atmospheric transport modeling + multi-station simultaneous detection + isotope ratio analysis = now standard; same methodology would detect Chernobyl-scale event within 2-4 hours globally

details: Nuclear explosion vs reactor accident forensic discrimination: key ratios: (1) Cs-134/Cs-137: weapons = 0 (single flash; no Cs-133 buildup); reactor = 0.3-0.6 depending on burnup; (2) I-131/Cs-137: weapons = high I/Cs (full fission yield 2.89% vs 6.19%); reactor = lower I/Cs (significant I-131 released from gaseous phase but Cs-137 retained longer in fuel → different fractions released); (3) Ru-103/Ru-106: weapons = high Ru-103 (t½=39d; abundant in fresh fission); old reactor release: lower Ru-103/Ru-106 (Ru-103 decayed if fuel old); (4) Ba-140/La-140: fresh weapons/reactor event → high Ba-140 (t½=12.75d); aged = gone; (5) Ba-133: surveillance tracer (CTBTO uses activation of Ba-132 target for event timing)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl 1986 sequence: CTBTO did not exist in 1986; Swedish Forsmark measurement on April 28: detected both Cs-137 and Cs-134 in ratio ~0.5; plus I-131; plus noble gases; BUT no Swedish reactor had leaked (checked same day); concluded = external source; ratio analysis pointed to: reactor accident (not weapons test) because Cs-134 present; burnup analysis: ~15,000 MWd/t (consistent with RBMK operation); geographic attribution: wind trajectory from E-SE = consistent with Soviet Union; forensic conclusion identical to what modern CTBTO would conclude; Forsmark scientist Leif Persson = first to reconstruct Chernobyl source from isotope ratios in real time
source: Persson 1987 J Environ Radioact; CTBTO PrepCom; Saey 2005 J Environ Radioact; fission_product_yields_REAL.csv

details: Source term back-calculation: atmospheric transport model inversion; given: measured air/deposition concentrations C(x,y,t) at N monitoring stations; model: Gaussian or Lagrangian transport model M(x,y,t|x_s,y_s,Q); inversion: minimize ||C_obs - M(Q)||² → Q(t) = time-varying source term; CTBTO uses this for treaty monitoring; for Chernobyl post-hoc analysis: SNAP-II/HYSPLIT backward trajectories from Forsmark → confirmed CEZ origin within hours of hypothetical notification; source term inversion using EURDEP network (2026): would reconstruct Chernobyl source term to within factor 2 from first 6 hours of data; accuracy limited by: meteorological model error; receptor coverage (gaps in eastern Europe); source height uncertainty
chernobyl_application: 1986 limitations: only ~200 monitoring stations in Europe (vs 5000+ EURDEP today); Soviet stations reported nothing; atmospheric model accuracy ~factor 2-5; actual source term (UNSCEAR 2008) agrees within ~30% with post-hoc inversions; SNAP-II model reconstruction by Persson 1987: estimated 10-100 PBq release from transport inversion → consistent with later estimates; modern IAEA ARGOS emergency response system: would have full source term reconstruction within 12hr of accident using current network density; CTBTO global treaty monitoring system (IMS): 337 stations; 80 noble gas detectors; 1-2hr detection latency

details: Sr-90 as forensic marker: Sr-90 has NO natural precursor (Sr-90 is not part of any natural decay series; U-238 chain does not produce Sr-90); therefore any Sr-90 in environment = exclusively from: (1) nuclear weapons testing 1945-1980; (2) reactor accidents (Chernobyl, Kyshtym, Windscale); (3) nuclear reprocessing effluents; Sr-90/Sr-89 ratio: Sr-89 t½=50.5d; Sr-90 t½=28.8yr; ratio decreases with time post-event; Sr-89/Sr-90 ratio at Chernobyl release (April 1986): 0.11 (from fission yields: Sr-89 yield 4.72% × specific activity / Sr-90 yield 5.82% × specific activity); Sr-89 = fully decayed by 1987; any Sr-90 found today = entirely Chernobyl+weapons (no Sr-89 remains from either source)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl vs weapons testing Sr-90 discrimination: geographic distribution = best tool; Chernobyl Sr-90 hot spots: <30km NW zone (>10 kBq/m²); weapons test Sr-90: globally distributed ~0.1-2 kBq/m² in 50-60°N latitude; contamination_zones_REAL.csv shows Chernobyl zone has Sr-90 10-1000x above weapons fallout background = easy discrimination; BOTH sources together = total environmental Sr-90 2026; current CEZ inner zone soil: Sr-90 hot spots 100-10,000 kBq/m² near Red Forest and NW particle deposition; surrounding Europe 0.1-0.5 kBq/m² weapons + 0.5-2 kBq/m² Chernobyl (500-2500km from CEZ)

details: Pu isotope ratio as burnup indicator: Pu-239 production: U-238 + n → U-239 → Np-239 → Pu-239; Pu-240 production: Pu-239 + n → Pu-240; Pu-241 production: Pu-240 + n → Pu-241; Pu-240/Pu-239 ratio (atom ratio) increases with burnup: 0 MWd/t: 0%; 1000 MWd/t (weapons Pu): ~5%; 10,000 MWd/t: ~20%; 15,000 MWd/t (Chernobyl): ~25-28%; 33,000 MWd/t (LWR standard): ~40-50%; Pu-240 specific activity = 8.40×10⁸ Bq/g; Pu-239 specific activity = 2.31×10⁹ Bq/g; activity ratio = atom ratio × (specific_activity_240 / specific_activity_239) × (molar_mass_ratio); forensic precision: ±2% absolute for atom ratio → ±2000 MWd/t burnup precision
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl Pu-240/239 atom ratio: calculated from ORIGEN code for 15,000 MWd/tHM RBMK-1000 → Pu-240/(Pu-239+240) = 26±2%; measured in CEZ soils: 26-28% (Ketterer 2004 measurement agrees); Fukushima Pu: different ratio (BWR fuel ~35,000 MWd/t; Pu-240 fraction ~40%); distinction between Chernobyl (unit 4 burnup ~15,000) and other sources = forensically clear; Pu-241: decays to Am-241 at rate proportional to Pu-241 inventory; current Am-241/Pu-239 activity ratio in CEZ soils (2026): ~0.22 (Am-241 40yr ingrowth from Pu-241); this ratio ALSO forensically attributable to Chernobyl burnup
